meta.title: Why safe retries need **idempotency**
meta.subject: Making payment webhooks safe to retry
meta.one_liner: Retrying is easy. Retrying without doing things twice is the real trick.

goal: By the end you can explain why a retry can charge a customer twice, and the two ideas that stop it from happening.
hook: A payment webhook was slow to answer, so the sender tried again. Now one customer has two receipts. Nothing was broken, yet something went wrong. What?

concepts.name: Retries with backoff
concepts.tagline: If at first you don't succeed, wait a bit longer and try again.
concepts.explain:
Messages between computers get lost or delayed all the time: a busy server, a dropped connection, a slow database. The sender can't tell "it failed" apart from "it worked but the answer got lost", so it plays safe and **sends again**.

Good senders wait longer after each failure (1s, 2s, 4s…). This is called **exponential backoff**, and it stops a struggling server from being buried under its own retries.
concepts.product: Retries are why payments, emails and notifications still arrive when the internet has a bad moment. The cost: the same message can arrive more than once, so every receiver must expect duplicates.
concepts.tech: Senders retry on timeouts and 5xx responses, usually with exponential backoff plus random jitter so thousands of clients don't retry in lockstep. Delivery is "at least once": duplicates are a feature of the protocol, not a bug.

examples.title: Calling a friend
examples.text: No answer? You call again in a few minutes, not every second. That pause is backoff.

examples.title: Webhook providers
examples.text: Payment and messaging platforms retry failed webhooks for hours or days, with growing gaps between attempts.

examples.title: Your slow webhook
examples.text: Your handler answered too slowly, so the provider assumed it failed and sent the same event again.

concepts.pitfall: Assuming each message arrives exactly once. With retries, "at least once" is the honest promise.

concepts.name: Idempotency
concepts.tagline: Doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once.
concepts.explain:
An action is **idempotent** when repeating it changes nothing after the first time. "Set the order status to paid" is idempotent. "Add ₹500 to the balance" is not.

The usual trick: every request carries a **unique key**. The receiver remembers keys it has handled, and when a key shows up again it returns the earlier result instead of redoing the work.
concepts.product: Customers never see double charges, duplicate emails or two identical orders, even when the network misbehaves. Ask engineers: "what happens if this request arrives twice?"
concepts.tech: Store a processed-request record keyed by the event or idempotency key. On arrival, look the key up first; if present, return the stored response. Keys need a retention window long enough to cover the sender's retry period.

examples.title: The lift button
examples.text: Pressing it five times still calls one lift. The button is idempotent.

examples.title: Idempotency keys in payment APIs
examples.text: Major payment APIs let you send an idempotency key with a charge, so retrying the same request never charges twice.

examples.title: Your event ID check
examples.text: Your handler now remembers each event ID and skips events it has already processed.

right.title: With idempotency
points: Second copy recognised by its ID

code.caption: The idea, simplified

concepts.pitfall: Using a timestamp or a random number as the key. A retry must carry the same key as the original, or the receiver can't recognise it.

concepts.name: Check and act atomically
concepts.tagline: "Have I done this?" and "do it" must happen as one step.
concepts.explain:
The simple version above has a gap. If two copies of the same event arrive at the **same moment**, both can ask "processed already?", both hear "no", and both charge.

The fix is to make the check and the action **atomic**: one indivisible step. Databases give you this with transactions and **unique constraints**: only one insert of a given event ID can ever succeed.
concepts.product: This is the difference between "usually no duplicates" and "never duplicates". It matters most for money, inventory and anything a customer can see.
concepts.tech: Insert the event ID into a table with a unique index inside the same transaction as the business write. The second concurrent insert fails on the constraint, and its transaction rolls back.

examples.title: Last concert ticket
examples.text: Two fans click Buy at the same instant. The box office must hand the ticket to exactly one of them, never both.

examples.title: Your single transaction
examples.text: Your event-ID insert and the order update now succeed or fail together, guarded by a unique index.

concepts.pitfall: Checking in application code first, then writing later. The gap between the two lines is exactly where the duplicate slips in.

connect.title: How the ideas fit together
connect.text: Retries make delivery reliable. Idempotency makes retries safe. Atomic checks make idempotency hold even under pressure.

quiz.question: Your server processed an event but crashed before replying. What will a well-behaved sender do?

options.why: The sender never got a reply, so it can't know that.

options.text: Send the same event again after a delay
options.why: No reply looks like failure, so it retries with backoff.

options.text: Send a new event with a new ID
options.why: Retries resend the same event. A new ID would defeat duplicate detection.

quiz.question: Which of these actions is idempotent?

options.text: Add one item to the cart
options.why: Doing it twice leaves two items.
Twice means two emails in the inbox.

options.text: Set the user's plan to Pro
options.why: After the first time, repeating it changes nothing.

quiz.question: A teammate generates a fresh random idempotency key on every retry attempt. What happens?

options.why: Each retry looks brand new to the receiver, so nothing is recognised.

options.text: It's safer, because keys never collide
options.why: Uniqueness per attempt is the problem: the key must be unique per action.
The receiver has no way to tell they are retries.

quiz.question: Two copies of one event arrive at the same millisecond. Both run "if not processed: charge". What stops a double charge?

options.text: Adding a short sleep before charging
options.why: Timing tricks shrink the gap; they don't close it.

options.text: A unique index on event ID, written in the same transaction as the charge
options.why: Only one insert can succeed, so only one charge commits.
Logs record the duplicate after it happens.

share.linkedin:
Learned something today that explains a lot of "charged twice" bugs.

Retries make systems reliable, but they also mean the same message can arrive more than once. The fix is idempotency: design actions so doing them twice has the same effect as once.

And the check has to be atomic, or two simultaneous retries can still slip through.
